native_result.query: How does the median wealth of white individuals compare to that of black and Hispanic individuals from 1985 onwards?
native_result.HypoA: 1985 onwards, white individuals have a significantly higher median wealth compared to black and Hispanic individuals.
native_result.HypoB: Among NLSY79 respondents, median family net wealth of non-black non-Hispanic ("white") respondents exceeded that of black and Hispanic respondents in every observed wave, and the gap widened monotonically across the only three wealth waves the file contains (1985, 1990, 1996 - "1985 onwards" here is three points, not a continuous trend). In constant 1996 USD (per-wave, unweighted, zeros and debts retained): white $5,104 (1985) -> $15,572 (1990) -> $42,600 (1996); black $2,333 -> $5,762 -> $9,800; Hispanic $729 -> $1,921 -> $2,562 (n = 5,774/1,699/2,631; 5,336/1,528/2,431; 3,557/1,368/2,114). The white/black median ratio was 2.19 [95% CI 1.83-2.47] -> 2.70 [2.31-3.25] -> 4.35 [3.70-5.20] and the white/Hispanic ratio 7.00 [5.70-8.75] -> 8.11 [6.36-9.13] -> 16.62 [13.83-21.30]; these ratios are scale-free, so they hold unchanged in nominal dollars, while the dollar gaps were $1,900 -> $8,172 -> $32,800 (white-black) and $3,000 -> $11,372 -> $40,038 (white-Hispanic) in nominal USD, i.e. the widening is fully visible without deflation; restating in 1996 USD only rescales the early waves (deflators 1.458 for 1985, 1.200 for 1990) to $2,771 -> $9,810 -> $32,800 and $4,375 -> $13,652 -> $40,038 - direction and ordering are identical in both money series. Every group's median rose in real terms (1985->1996: white +735%, black +320%, Hispanic +251%), so the divergence is relative: white wealth grew roughly twice as fast as black and nearly three times as fast as Hispanic. The distribution corroborates this: net wealth was <= 0 for 19.2/16.4/10.9% of white families versus 28.4/25.5/20.8% of black families (-9 to -10 pp) and 41.9/33.8/34.9% of Hispanic families (-17 to -24 pp). Caveats: this is family-level net wealth of the respondent/spouse (in 1985, respondents were only 20-28, so many are parental households), unweighted, with black and Hispanic oversamples (15.8% and 25.0% of the sample), so absolute levels are not US-representative even though group contrasts remain informative; wealth is observed for 76.9% of whites versus 84.9% of blacks and 82.9% of Hispanics in 1985, falling to 47.4% versus 68.3% and 66.6% in 1996 (only 61.6% of the 1985-observed whites versus ~80% of blacks/Hispanics remain observed), so waves are partly different people - yet the balanced panel of 5,739 respondents with all three waves gives the same ordering and slightly LARGER ratios (1996: 4.69 white/black, 17.75 white/Hispanic), because white 1996 medians are flat across retention groups ($42,600 stayers vs $42,000 non-stayers) while non-staying black/Hispanic respondents were richer ($11,918/$4,500 vs stayers $9,075/$2,400); differential attrition therefore understates rather than inflates the 1996 gap. Finally, the white/Hispanic ratio is not scale-robust (the Hispanic median sits one reporting-rounding step above zero; positive-wealth-only medians cut it to 2.24 in 1985 and 5.17 in 1996, while the dollar gap is stable at $4,520 and $43,000), so for that contrast the absolute difference and the share with non-positive wealth are the load-bearing statistics; the apparent top-coding at the maxima (84 observations at $1,321,099 in 1990 and 141 at $1,232,183 in 1996) is a plausible interpretation, not a documented fact, and it shifts means but leaves medians and 5%-trimmed medians unchanged.

sub_hypo.relations: Constant-1996 USD medians rose from $5,104 to $15,572 to $42,600 for whites, $2,333 to $5,762 to $9,800 for blacks, and $729 to $1,921 to $2,562 for Hispanics. Nominal white–black gaps increased $1,900 → $8,172 → $32,800, and white–Hispanic gaps increased $3,000 → $11,372 → $40,038. Corresponding real gaps were $2,771 → $9,810 → $32,800 and $4,375 → $13,652 → $40,038. Ratios are unchanged by per-wave deflation, and gap direction and ordering agree in nominal and real dollars. Confidence intervals were estimated using 1,000 bootstrap replicates.

sub_hypo.text: All three groups experienced rising real median family wealth, but white respondents experienced substantially faster proportional growth.
sub_hypo.context: Unweighted NLSY79 per-wave wealth observations in 1985, 1990, and 1996, expressed in constant-1996 USD with zeros and debts retained; waves contain partly different respondents.
sub_hypo.relations: Every group's real median increased across both observed intervals. From 1985 to 1996, white median wealth rose 735%, black median wealth 320%, and Hispanic median wealth 251%; white proportional growth was roughly twice black growth and nearly three times Hispanic growth. Divergence therefore occurred despite rising medians in every group.

sub_hypo.text: White families consistently had a lower share of non-positive net wealth than black and Hispanic families.
sub_hypo.context: Unweighted NLSY79 respondents with observed family wealth in 1985, 1990, and 1996; non-positive wealth includes zero wealth and net debt.
sub_hypo.relations: Shares with wealth ≤ 0 were 19.2% → 16.4% → 10.9% for whites, 28.4% → 25.5% → 20.8% for blacks, and 41.9% → 33.8% → 34.9% for Hispanics. White shares were approximately 9–10 percentage points below black shares and 17–24 points below Hispanic shares. White and black shares declined monotonically; the Hispanic share declined initially and then increased.

sub_hypo.text: Wealth observation and retention differed by racial/ethnic cohort, with particularly pronounced loss of observed wealth among white respondents.
sub_hypo.context: NLSY79 cohort-by-wave attrition and item-non-response analysis across the three wealth waves; per-wave comparisons are not a fully balanced panel.
sub_hypo.relations: Wealth was observed for 76.9% of whites, 84.9% of blacks, and 82.9% of Hispanics in 1985, falling to 47.4%, 68.3%, and 66.6%, respectively, in 1996. Only 61.6% of whites observed in 1985 remained observed in 1996, compared with approximately 80% of blacks and Hispanics.

sub_hypo.text: Balanced-panel comparisons preserve the racial/ethnic wealth ordering and suggest that differential attrition understates rather than inflates the 1996 wealth gaps.
sub_hypo.context: NLSY79 balanced panel of 5,739 respondents with wealth observed in all three waves, compared with per-wave samples and retention groups; unweighted wealth comparisons.
sub_hypo.relations: The balanced panel retains the same ordering and yields slightly larger 1996 median ratios: 4.69 white/black and 17.75 white/Hispanic. This selection pattern supports understatement rather than inflation of the 1996 disparities.

sub_hypo.text: The white/Hispanic median wealth ratio is sensitive to the near-zero Hispanic median and positive-wealth restriction, making absolute gaps and non-positive-wealth shares more reliable summaries of that contrast.
sub_hypo.context: NLSY79 white and Hispanic respondents; comparison of the main unweighted analysis retaining zeros and debts with positive-wealth-only sensitivity analysis. The Hispanic median is one reporting-rounding step above zero.
sub_hypo.relations: Restricting to positive wealth reduces the white/Hispanic median ratio from 7.00 to 2.24 in 1985 and from 16.62 to 5.17 in 1996, while the reported dollar gaps remain comparatively stable at $4,520 and $43,000. Thus invariance to nominal-versus-real currency conversion does not imply robustness to near-zero denominators or sample restriction. The workflow flags denominator confidence intervals containing zero or width greater than 25 times the denominator.

sub_hypo.text: Concentrations at the maximum recorded wealth values suggest possible top-coding, but this is not documented; the apparent top-coding affects means without changing medians or 5%-trimmed medians.
sub_hypo.context: NLSY79 wealth-distribution sensitivity analysis, including means, medians, 5%-trimmed medians, and two-sided 1st/99th-percentile winsorisation; apparent top-coding is an interpretation rather than an established data feature.
sub_hypo.relations: There are 84 observations at the 1990 maximum of $1,321,099 and 141 at the 1996 maximum of $1,232,183. The hypothesized upper-tail coding shifts means but leaves medians and 5%-trimmed medians unchanged.
